# Pitting Potential (EPIT)
## A Measure of Pitting Resistance

![Diagram of pitting corrosion beneath a damaged passive film](pitting-corrosion-diagram-1.png)

- **Pitting corrosion:** local breakdown of the protective passive film allows pits to form.
- **EPIT:** the electrochemical potential at which breakdown or sustained pitting is detected during a test.
- **Higher EPIT $\rightarrow$ greater resistance to pit initiation**, under comparable conditions.
- EPIT depends on the **alloy, material state, environment, and test procedure**.

---

<!-- _footer: "Source: Nyby et al. (2021), Electrochemical Metrics for Corrosion Resistant Alloys, Figshare." -->

# From Alloy Composition and Test Conditions to EPIT

**760 rows · 21 input variables · 1 prediction target**

- **Composition:** 17 element weight percentages, including Fe, Cr, Ni, Mo, and W.
- **Test conditions:** temperature, chloride concentration, pH, and experimental method.
- **Target:** average pitting potential, measured in **mV vs SCE**.

<!--
Each row describes an alloy tested under particular conditions. We use its composition

Ni–Cr–Mo, Al, high-entropy, and other alloys.

# How a Conventional Machine-Learning Model Works

- A model is trained directly on the available dataset.
- During training, it compares predictions with known target values and adjusts its parameters.
- The result is one model fitted specifically to that dataset.
- A different target or dataset normally requires new training.

$$
(x,y)\xrightarrow{\text{fitting}}\text{fitted model},
\qquad
(\text{fitted model},x^\ast)\longrightarrow y^\ast
$$

---

# A Model Pretrained to Learn from Tables

- **Tabular foundation models such as TabPFN and TabICL are gaining attention, often outperforming conventional models on benchmark datasets.**
- TabICL is pretrained before seeing the real EPIT task.
- Pretraining uses many automatically generated synthetic tables.
- These tables have different relationships between features and target.
- **The model still needs labeled EPIT examples.** It uses them as context during prediction rather than to retrain its parameters.

$$
\underbrace{D_1,D_2,\ldots,D_N}_{\text{Synthetic tables}}
\xrightarrow{\text{pretraining}}
\underbrace{\text{TabICL}_{\phi}}_{\text{Learned weights }\phi}
$$

$$
(x,y,x^\ast)
\xrightarrow{\text{pretrained TabICL}}
q_\phi(y^\ast\mid x^\ast,x,y)
$$

# How TabICL Builds a Prediction

TabICL uses **attention** to learn how to combine information from features and examples.

- **Column:** use other values in the column to give each value context.
- **Row:** combine its features into a representation of the whole row.
- **Examples:** use rows with known targets to guide predictions for new rows.
- **Training:** compare predictions with the generated targets and update the model’s parameters.

# The Case for an Informed Prior

- Generic TabICL sees anonymous columns such as $X_1, X_2, \ldots$.
- It does not know which feature represents chromium, chloride, temperature, or test method.
- Its synthetic target has no pitting-potential interpretation.
- It learns general statistical patterns, but its synthetic training contains no deliberate corrosion structure.

> **Central project idea:** Make some synthetic training tasks more relevant to EPIT by including alloy compositions, test conditions, and corrosion-inspired relationships.

# Our Corrosion-Informed Implementation

## Corrosion-relevant input distributions

- **Alloy compositions:** sample recorded Fe and Ni–Cr–Mo compositions and introduce random variations.
- **Test conditions:** sample recorded combinations of temperature, chloride concentration, pH, and test method.

## Corrosion-informed target formulas

- A random SCM has no built-in reason to link higher chloride with lower pitting resistance.
- We add formulas that calculate a target score from **alloy composition and test conditions**.
- These formulas express corrosion tendencies from the literature: **material protection raises the score; environmental aggressiveness lowers it**.

## Seven rules

- Linear PREN-inspired
- Cr–Mo/W synergy
- Threshold and saturation
- Separate environmental effects
- Coupled breakdown
- Fe/Ni chromium threshold
- Method-aware

# Example: Separate environmental effects

$$
y_{\mathrm{rule}}=aP-bC-cH-dI-eA
$$

- **$P$:** material protection, based on $\mathrm{Cr}+3.25(\mathrm{Mo}+0.55\,\mathrm{W})$.
- **$C$:** chloride aggressiveness, based on log concentration.
- **$H$:** a penalty that increases with temperature.
- **$I$:** an additional penalty when temperature and chloride are both high.
- **$A$:** a penalty that increases as pH decreases.

The coefficients $a,b,c,d,e$ control the strength of each contribution.

1. Fit formula weights to match measured EPIT rankings in development data.
2. Choose one of seven formulas per synthetic table, favoring those that perform better on validation data.
3. Standardize and combine the chosen rule’s target value with the original generator’s target value.

# Mean Validation Spearman Scores of Each Rule

| Rule | Score |
| --- | ---: |
| Linear PREN-inspired | 0.5174 |
| Cr–Mo/W synergy | 0.5583 |
| Threshold and saturation | 0.5181 |
| Separate environmental effects | 0.5850 |
| Coupled breakdown | 0.5525 |
| Fe/Ni chromium threshold | 0.5252 |
| **Method-aware** | **0.5999** |

- Applied each rule to real corrosion rows excluded from fitting.
- Calculated the Spearman correlation between rule scores and measured EPIT values.
- Averaged the correlations across five folds.

# Optuna: Best Trial and Parameters

- Optuna compared settings using **1,000-step training runs**.
- **Best completed trial: 56.**
- **Mean validation Spearman: 0.6903**, averaged across five development folds.

| Parameter | Selected value |
| --- | --- |
| Share of corrosion-informed tables | **75%** informed, 25% original generator |
| Composition variation strength | **0.1028** |
| Generator within informed tables | **50% MLP, 50% tree** |
| Rule weight in the combined target | **20.48% rule, 79.52% original generator** |

# Comparison Models and Testing

| Model | Training |
| --- | --- |
| **Generic TabICL** | Trained from scratch: V2 architecture, V1 data generator. |
| **Pretrained TabICL V2** | Authors’ pretrained weights: V2 architecture and V2 data generator. |
| **CatBoost** | Trained directly on real EPIT data. |

- Split development folds and the final-test set mainly by **alloy composition** to reduce data leakage.
- Used development rows as **labeled context** and final-test rows as **queries with unseen EPIT targets**.
- Final-test targets were **not used to fit formulas, update model parameters, or select settings**.

# Appendix · 1. Linear PREN-Inspired

$$
y=aP-bE-cI_{\mathrm{MC}}
$$

- **$P$ — material protection:** based on $\mathrm{Cr}+\alpha(\mathrm{Mo}+\eta\,\mathrm{W})$.
- **$E$ — environmental aggressiveness:** combines chloride, temperature, and pH.
- **$I_{\mathrm{MC}}$ — material–chloride interaction:** increases when protection is weak and chloride is high.

**Idea:** Cr, Mo, and W improve pitting resistance; aggressive conditions and weak protection lower the target score.

---

<style scoped>
section { padding: 40px 50px; font-size: 27px; line-height: 1.35; }
h1 { font-size: 38px; margin: 0 0 24px; }
ul { margin: 20px 0; padding-left: 1.15em; }
li + li { margin-top: 0.5em; }
</style>

# Appendix · 2. Cr–Mo/W Synergy

$$
y=aP_{\mathrm{syn}}-bE-cI_{\mathrm{MC}}-dI_{\mathrm{TC}}
$$

- **$P_{\mathrm{syn}}$ — cooperative protection:** based on $\mathrm{Cr}+\alpha q+\beta\sqrt{\mathrm{Cr}\,q}$, with $q=\mathrm{Mo}+\eta\,\mathrm{W}$.
- **$E$ and $I_{\mathrm{MC}}$:** environmental aggressiveness and the weak-protection/chloride interaction.
- **$I_{\mathrm{TC}}$:** an extra penalty when temperature and chloride are both high.

**Idea:** Chromium and Mo/W can reinforce each other's protective effect; their joint benefit exceeds the additive contribution.

---

<style scoped>
section { padding: 40px 50px; font-size: 27px; line-height: 1.35; }
h1 { font-size: 38px; margin: 0 0 24px; }
ul { margin: 20px 0; padding-left: 1.15em; }
li + li { margin-top: 0.5em; }
</style>

# Appendix · 3. Threshold and Saturation

$$
y=aP_{\mathrm{sat}}-bE-cI_{\mathrm{MC}}-dI_{\mathrm{TC}}
$$

- **$P_{\mathrm{sat}}$ — nonlinear protection:** based on $\sigma((\mathrm{Cr}-\theta)/s)+\ln(1+q/q_0)$, with $q=\mathrm{Mo}+\eta\,\mathrm{W}$.
- **$\sigma$** is a smooth sigmoid: protection rises around chromium threshold $\theta$; the logarithm gives diminishing Mo/W returns.
- **$E$, $I_{\mathrm{MC}}$, $I_{\mathrm{TC}}$:** environment, weak-protection/chloride, and temperature/chloride penalties.

**Idea:** Chromium protection rises around a passivation threshold, while additional Mo/W gives diminishing benefits.

---

<style scoped>
section { padding: 40px 50px; font-size: 27px; line-height: 1.35; }
h1 { font-size: 38px; margin: 0 0 24px; }
ul { margin: 20px 0; padding-left: 1.15em; }
li + li { margin-top: 0.5em; }
</style>

# Appendix · 4. Separate Environmental Effects

$$
y=aP-bC-cH-dI_{\mathrm{TC}}-eA
$$

- **$P$:** material protection based on Cr, Mo, and W.
- **$C$ and $H$:** separate chloride and high-temperature penalties.
- **$I_{\mathrm{TC}}$:** additional penalty when chloride and temperature are both high.
- **$A$:** acidic-pH penalty.

**Idea:** Give each environmental effect its own weight so chloride, temperature, their interaction, and acidity can contribute differently.

---

<style scoped>
section { padding: 40px 50px; font-size: 27px; line-height: 1.35; }
h1 { font-size: 38px; margin: 0 0 24px; }
ul { margin: 20px 0; padding-left: 1.15em; }
li + li { margin-top: 0.5em; }
</style>

# Appendix · 5. Coupled Breakdown

$$
y=aP-bB-cA,\qquad B=\sigma(G-\gamma M)
$$

- **$P$ and $M$:** protection and its underlying standardized Cr–Mo/W material signal.
- **$G$:** combined aggressiveness from chloride, high temperature, and their interaction.
- **$B$:** smooth breakdown response; it grows as aggressiveness exceeds material protection.
- **$A$:** acidic-pH penalty.

**Idea:** The same environment causes more breakdown in a weakly protected alloy. Stronger material protection shifts the breakdown threshold.

---

<style scoped>
section { padding: 40px 50px; font-size: 27px; line-height: 1.35; }
h1 { font-size: 38px; margin: 0 0 24px; }
ul { margin: 20px 0; padding-left: 1.15em; }
li + li { margin-top: 0.5em; }
</style>

# Appendix · 6. Fe/Ni Chromium Threshold

$$
y=aP_f-bC-cH-dI_{\mathrm{TC}}-eA
$$

- **$P_f$ — family-specific protection:** based on $\sigma((\mathrm{Cr}-\theta_f)/s)+\ln(1+q/q_0)$, with $q=\mathrm{Mo}+\eta\,\mathrm{W}$.
- **$\theta_f$:** a lower chromium threshold for Fe alloys and a higher one for Ni–Cr–Mo alloys.
- **$C$, $H$, $I_{\mathrm{TC}}$, $A$:** separate chloride, high-temperature, joint, and acidic-pH penalties.

**Idea:** Fe and Ni–Cr–Mo alloys need different chromium thresholds to develop protection.

---

<style scoped>
section { padding: 40px 50px; font-size: 27px; line-height: 1.35; }
h1 { font-size: 38px; margin: 0 0 24px; }
ul { margin: 20px 0; padding-left: 1.15em; }
li + li { margin-top: 0.5em; }
</style>

# Appendix · 7. Method-Aware

$$
y=aP_{\mathrm{syn}}-bE-cI_{\mathrm{MC}}-dI_{\mathrm{TC}}+eD_m
$$

- **$P_{\mathrm{syn}}$:** Cr–Mo/W synergy protection.
- **$E$, $I_{\mathrm{MC}}$, $I_{\mathrm{TC}}$:** environmental and interaction penalties.
- **$D_m$:** an offset associated with the test method; rows measured by the same method share it.
- Synthetic tables receive newly sampled method offsets.

**Idea:** Experimental methods can shift the target score even when alloy composition and environmental conditions are similar.
